opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, the thing I value most is that they're incredibly rigorous, and that rigor makes us better. Pharmaceutical scientists live in a world where being wrong is expensive, sometimes years and hundreds of millions of dollars expensive, so they don't get dazzled by a slick demo. They want to know how a model was validated, what the failure modes are, where the uncertainty lives. That pushback is a gift. It forces you to build things that actually hold up rather than things that just look good on a benchmark.

The second thing is that they bring deep domain intuition that no amount of data replaces. A medicinal chemist who's been doing this for twenty years can look at a molecule a model proposes and tell you in five seconds, "That's going to be a nightmare to synthesize," or "That scaffold has a metabolic liability." Early on, we'd sometimes treat that kind of feedback as anecdotal. Now we treat it as signal, and some of our best product decisions came directly from sitting next to chemists and biologists and watching where they hesitated.

And third, they're genuinely mission-driven. At the end of the day, everyone in the room wants the same thing, which is getting better medicines to patients faster. That shared goal makes the relationship feel less like vendor and customer and more like collaborators. When something doesn't work, the conversation isn't about blame. It's "okay, what did we learn, and what do we try next?" That's a really healthy culture to build a company around.

r002.rationale: It describes scientists’ deep domain intuition about molecules and liabilities as valuable feedback that directly informs product decisions.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, what I value most is that they don't let you get away with anything. If you walk into a room of medicinal chemists or clinical pharmacologists and say "the model is 92% accurate," the first question is "accurate at what, on which distribution, and what happens on the 8%?" They've spent their careers in a world where a wrong answer doesn't just cost you a bad demo, it costs years and real money and sometimes patient safety. So the bar for evidence is just fundamentally different from what I was used to in software.

And that's uncomfortable at first, but it makes the product better. They force you to be precise about failure modes. They care about provenance, where did this claim come from, can I trace it back to the assay or the paper. They want to know what the model doesn't know. A lot of AI products are built for users who want a confident answer. These people want a calibrated one, and they can tell the difference.

The other thing I'd say is that they're incredibly generous with domain knowledge once they trust you. A scientist who's been doing ADME work for twenty years will sit with you for an hour and explain why a particular metric is misleading, and that hour is worth more than a month of reading. There's a real craft tradition there, a lot of tacit knowledge that never made it into any dataset, and getting to learn from that directly is one of the best parts of the job.

So yeah, demanding customers, but the demanding part is the point. If you can build something they'll actually rely on, you've built something real.

r002.rationale: It says scientists share domain knowledge that makes the product better, including explaining why metrics are misleading and contributing tacit research expertise.

And the underlying goal—helping develop better medicines—is a pretty compelling reason to do the work.

If you can help them spend less time on repetitive tasks and more time doing science, that’s a pretty compelling thing to build toward.
